title: The first balloon passengers
hook: The first passengers in a hot-air balloon were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
peek: In September 1783, the Montgolfier brothers sent a balloon up at Versailles in front of King Louis XVI. In the basket were a sheep, a duck and a rooster, sent to test whether living things could breathe up in the sky. All three came down safely.
lede: In 1783 nobody knew whether the air high above the ground was safe to breathe. Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier, paper makers from Annonay in France, had already flown an unmanned hot-air balloon. Before risking a person, they sent up three animals at the Palace of Versailles on 19 September, with King Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette watching.

bullets.text: The balloon carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster in a basket. It flew for about eight minutes and came down a few kilometres away in a wood. All three animals were found alive.

The sheep was thought to be a fair stand-in for a person. The duck, a bird used to flying high, acted as a comparison, and the rooster was a bird that does not fly high. If all three survived, the air up there was safe.
The sheep's name is usually given as Montauciel, meaning climb to the sky. Afterwards, the story goes, it lived out its days in the queen's menagerie.
The Montgolfiers believed their balloons rose because of a special gas in smoke, so they burned straw and wool. The real reason was simpler: hot air is lighter than cool air.
Two months later, on 21 November 1783, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes flew over Paris for about 25 minutes, becoming the first people to fly.
